vignette:
She is seventy-eight now, a widowed African woman who has spent most of her life shaping clay with steady hands. Before the assault, her days follow a rhythm she trusts. She wakes before sunrise, sweeps the yard, boils tea, and walks to the small workshop behind her house where rows of bowls and water jars dry in the morning air. Since her husband's death years ago, the work has become more than a livelihood. It gives shape to long days and keeps loneliness from hardening inside her. Neighbors know her as quiet but warm, a woman whose hands can coax beauty from mud.

The assault happens in the late afternoon as she closes the workshop. A man she vaguely recognizes from the area comes asking to buy a pot. She turns back to show him the shelves, and in that small moment the day changes. He forces his way inside, shoves her against the table, and strikes her when she cries out. She remembers the smell of damp clay, one bowl shattering on the floor, and the shock of finding herself pinned in the very place that has always felt safest. More than the pain, she remembers the disbelief-that at her age, in her own yard, this can still happen. When he leaves, she stays on the ground for a long time, too stunned to stand, her cheek pressed against cool dust.

In the first weeks afterward, she tells almost no one. Shame settles over her faster than bruises. She washes herself repeatedly, scrubbing her arms until the skin stings. At night she bolts the door, then checks it again and again, sometimes six or seven times before lying down. Sleep does not really come. When it does, she jerks awake drenched in sweat, hearing again the crash of pottery and the scrape of shoes on the floor. In the dark she sits upright, listening for footsteps that are not there. Roosters crow at dawn before she realizes she has not slept at all.

She tries to return to pottery because it is what she knows, but the workshop has changed. The doorway feels narrow, the room airless. When she bends over wet clay, the smell takes her back so suddenly that her chest tightens and her hands begin to tremble. She leaves lumps of clay unfinished on the wheel. Bowls collapse under her fingers because she can no longer keep pressure steady. She tells customers her eyes are weak now, that age is slowing her work, but privately she knows it is fear. Some afternoons she stands outside the workshop, keys in hand, unable to make herself go in.

Her world grows smaller. She stops going alone to the market and asks a niece to buy supplies. If men gather near the road, even laughing among themselves, she crosses to the other side or turns back home. Unexpected noises-a dropped pan, a knock at the gate, a motorcycle engine sputtering-make her jump so hard that she presses a hand to her chest. She has become watchful in a way that exhausts her. Even while drinking tea with relatives, part of her is listening, scanning, calculating exits.

She is troubled too by how the assault has changed the way she sees herself. She has survived widowhood, childbirth, poverty, political unrest, and the losses that come with old age. She has always thought of herself as durable. Now she feels fragile and angry at her own fragility. Sometimes she scolds herself-You are an old woman, why are you still afraid?-but the fear does not obey reason. She cries in private, mostly in the workshop, surrounded by unfinished pots she no longer trusts herself to complete.

There are moments when memory intrudes without warning. While kneading clay, she sees his arm coming toward her. While hearing a customer ask for a water jar, she remembers trying to call out and not being able to make her voice work. On bad days she loses pieces of time, staring at the wall until the tea has gone cold beside her. Relatives notice she is more distant. She misses family gatherings, saying her joints hurt. In truth, the noise and movement overwhelm her, and she cannot bear the questions about why she no longer smiles easily.

Now, months later, she still lives in the same house and still keeps the workshop, though she uses only part of it. She works in short stretches during daylight and closes well before evening. She sits with her back to the wall and the door in sight. She says the clay used to feel alive in her hands; now it sometimes feels heavy, stubborn, like something she must struggle to bring into form. Yet she continues, shaping small bowls, one after another, as if repetition might restore a sense of order. She does not talk about the assault easily, but when she does, her voice flattens and her gaze fixes on the floor. Underneath that restraint is a constant tension, as though some part of her remains in that late afternoon, still listening for danger in the room that once felt like home.
